name: delegation
intent: Handle a request you do not implement yourself by deferring it to a contained delegate, so behaviour is reused by composition instead of inheritance: an object can be composed from, extended around or substituted for an implementation without inheriting its interface or its implementation. Unlike plain forwarding (where the member runs in the delegate's own context), true delegation makes the sender's context available to the delegate - by passing the receiver explicitly or by a language mechanism - so the delegate's self-references resolve back through the wrapper.
problem: A class needs behaviour that already exists in another type, but inheriting that type would drag in its whole interface and implementation: the subclass is bound to the base at compile time, cannot vary the reused behaviour per instance, cannot reuse two implementations at once under single inheritance, and inherits every future change to the base (the fragile base class problem). The same reuse is wanted by several unrelated classes that share no usable base class at all.
context: Applies wherever 'uses' is masquerading as 'is-a': wrappers that add behaviour (validation, logging, caching, retry) around an implementation, interchangeable algorithm or state objects, adapters between layers or foreign APIs, framework classes that must not be subclassed, and code that must reuse two implementations where the language allows only one base class. It is also the only reuse mechanism in languages without implementation inheritance (Go, Rust) and the one that Kotlin (`by`), Scala 3 (`export`) and Ruby (`Forwardable`/`SimpleDelegator`) generate from a declaration.
benefits: Reuse without a subtype relationship: the wrapper can present a narrower, wider or different interface than the delegate, so an implementation can be reused without becoming part of the client's type hierarchy.

Black-box reuse: only the delegate's interface is depended on, never its internals, so changes inside the delegate cannot silently change the wrapper's behaviour and no fragile-base-class coupling is created.
Per-instance variation: the delegate can be selected, injected or replaced at runtime (Strategy, State, Decorator), which inheritance, being a class-level relationship, cannot express.

Composition scales where inheritance does not: a wrapper can delegate to several collaborators, so an application can reuse two implementations at once without multiple-inheritance diamonds or an occupied single-inheritance slot.
Explicit control at the seam: every forwarded call passes through wrapper code, which is where validation, conversion, logging, caching or retries are added without touching the delegate.
Testability: because the delegate is supplied through a constructor or setter, a stub, spy or fake can be put in its place at the seam.
tradeoffs: Forwarding boilerplate: unless the language generates it (Kotlin `by`, Go embedding, Ruby `Forwardable`), every forwarded member is written by hand and must be updated when the delegate's interface grows - a missed member is a compile error at best, a silently absent feature at worst.

Identity and self-reference change: with inheritance `this`/`self` is the object under extension, but with delegation the delegate still talks about itself, so calls it makes to its own members never see the wrapper's overrides (the reason the GoF note that to get inheritance-like reuse the receiver must be handed to the delegate).

Extra indirection per call: one more object to hold and one more dispatch (virtual, closure or reflective) per forwarded operation, which defeats devirtualisation in the delegate and costs a heap allocation in callable-based realizations.

Interface coupling remains: the wrapper is decoupled from the delegate's implementation, but not from its interface - a change there forces the wrapper, and every other wrapper of the same type, to be edited.

Contract risk: nothing in the type system keeps the wrapper's semantics compatible with the delegate's, so substitutability becomes a documentation-and-tests property rather than a compiler-checked one.

Ownership and aliasing become explicit: someone must own the delegate, decide whether it may be shared and keep it alive; two wrappers around one mutable delegate observe each other's effects, and a stale delegate reference is a dangling or logically dead object.

Missing a forwarded method is silent: in hand-written forwarding, a method added to the delegate's interface but not to the wrapper surfaces only at call sites that use the new method, not at the wrapper's definition.
Thread safety of shared delegates: mutable delegates shared across wrappers or threads require their own synchronization, which is invisible at the wrapper's call site.

participants.responsibility: Owns or references the delegate, exposes the interface the client uses and forwards the requests it does not handle itself.

The contained object that performs the forwarded work; it may be unaware of the wrapper, or, in the stronger (prototype-style) form of delegation, be handed the receiver explicitly so that self-references resolve to the wrapper.
The shared abstraction (class, interface, protocol, trait) that makes the wrapper usable wherever the delegate is expected, so clients never have to know about the delegate.
Calls the receiving object and must not need to know that a delegate exists - that is what makes the wrapper substitutable and the delegate replaceable.

use_cases: Adding cross-cutting behaviour around an existing implementation: caching, retry, logging or validation wrappers over repositories, HTTP clients, streams or file stores (the Decorator/Proxy family).
Interchangeable behaviour per instance: Strategy and State objects a context forwards to, so the same context type behaves differently per instance or after a state change.

Breaking an is-implemented-in-terms-of inheritance: a class that used to extend a concrete container or collection and now holds it as a member (a Stack over a list, a Set over a map), exposing only the intended operations.
Narrow facades over large or foreign APIs: a wrapper that exposes a handful of methods of a subsystem, JDBC connection or vendor SDK and forwards only those.
Adapting a foreign object to an interface the client owns (Adapter/Bridge), including cases where the foreign class cannot be changed to implement a protocol or trait.
Delegating test doubles: a wrapper that forwards to the real object while recording or modifying calls, used where a full mock would duplicate the delegate's behaviour.

UI event handling: event bubbling in graphical toolkits (Java AWT, Swing, DOM) delegates event dispatch to a parent widget that traverses the component hierarchy, rather than each leaf component handling every event.

Microservices and middleware: an API gateway or service mesh sidecar proxies requests to an upstream service, adding authentication, rate-limiting or retries - structurally identical to the Proxy pattern but often implemented as infrastructure rather than application code.

Dependency injection containers: a container resolves a dependency graph and injects implementations into constructors or fields; the injected object is used directly by the consumer, which is delegation without a visible wrapper.

Composition of read and write repositories: a `ReadWriteRepository` holds separate `ReadRepository` and `WriteRepository` delegates and routes `find`/`save` calls to the appropriate one, combining two interfaces into one without shared inheritance.
Android touch event handling: View.java uses an `inputEventDispatcher` delegate to forward touch events to the appropriate view, enabling event bubbling without inheritance coupling.

UIKit/AppKit delegation: iOS and macOS frameworks use formal protocol-based delegation extensively (UITableViewDelegate, NSTableViewDelegate) where the delegating object forwards lifecycle and interaction callbacks to a delegate object.

Python `__getattr__` delegation: Using `__getattr__` to forward any unknown attribute access to an inner implementation object, creating a generic proxy that works for any interface — see python-3-patterns-idioms-test.readthedocs.io.

Fast.ai GetAttr pattern: A base class that propagates attribute access to a wrapped inner object by default, fixing Python's __getattr__ limitation where instance attributes shadow the inner object's attributes.

Event bus and message brokers: Publishers delegate message delivery to a broker that routes to subscribers, decoupling the sender from receivers (structurally similar to Observer but operates at the service/infrastructure layer).
Database connection pooling: A pool holds reusable connections and delegates queries to an available connection, adding lifecycle management without the caller managing connections directly.

Reverse proxy and API gateways: An ingress service delegates incoming requests to upstream services, adding auth, rate-limiting, or logging at the seam — identical structure to Proxy at infrastructure scale.
Test spy recording: A test double wraps a real object and records calls while forwarding them, allowing assertions on interaction history without duplicating the object's behaviour in a mock.

Rails ActiveSupport's `delegate` macro: `delegate :name, to: :user` generates forwarding methods to a contained object or association (with `prefix`, `allow_nil` and `private` options), and `delegate_missing_to` forwards everything the receiver does not define — delegation as a first-class framework feature.

Google Guava's ForwardingObject family (ForwardingList, ForwardingMap, ForwardingCollection): abstract `delegate()` plus a generated forwarder per collection method, the canonical Java library for wrapping a collection while overriding only the methods you change.

Prototype-based languages as language-level delegation: JavaScript's prototype chain and Self's delegates retry a failed member lookup on the prototype with `self` still bound to the original receiver, the mechanism Lieberman proposed in OOPSLA '86 as a dynamic alternative to inheritance.
avoid_when: The relationship is genuinely is-a and the base type's contract is meant to be inherited and substituted: plain public or interface inheritance is simpler, allocation-free and checked by the compiler.

The language already generates the forwarding you need: use Kotlin `by`, Go embedding or Ruby `Forwardable` instead of writing forwarders by hand, and remember they forward everything unless overridden.
Only a single operation has to be reused: pass a function, closure or callable (function composition, a lambda strategy) instead of building a wrapper object and an interface for it.
The wrapper adds no behaviour of its own and repeats the delegate's members one-to-one: that is a middle man (Lazy Class/Middle Man smell) and the delegate should be used directly.
The reused code must observe the wrapper's overrides: self-calls inside the delegate stay inside the delegate, so public inheritance or explicitly passing the receiver is the honest mechanism.

The delegate's interface is wide and rapidly evolving: hand-written forwarders accumulate maintenance debt every time the interface changes; prefer narrowing the exposed surface or a language with generated forwarding.
The wrapper and delegate are in the same package/module and share the same release cadence: tight temporal coupling between them means the indirection buys less than it costs.

related_patterns_notes.strategy: Strategy also uses delegation - a context holds a strategy object and forwards algorithmic work to it. The difference is intent: delegation is the reuse mechanism; Strategy is one specific arrangement where the delegate is an interchangeable algorithm selected at runtime. Every Strategy uses delegation; not every delegation is a Strategy.
related_patterns_notes.decorator: Decorator is delegation plus the intent to add behaviour (logging, caching, buffering) at runtime, often stacking multiple decorators on one component. Both share the same interface as the wrapped object. Delegation is the structural mechanism; Decorator is one purpose it serves.
related_patterns_notes.adapter: Adapter uses delegation to translate an incompatible interface into one the client expects. An adapter wrapping a foreign SDK forwards calls but may translate parameters and return values; a plain delegation wrapper shares the same interface without translation. Adapter's purpose is interface compatibility; Delegation's purpose is reuse.
related_patterns_notes.state: State uses delegation to let a context forward behaviour to a state object that encapsulates how the context should behave in a given state. The delegate is swapped on state transitions. Like Strategy, State exploits the per-instance variation that delegation enables; the distinction is that State models an object's lifecycle phases, not alternative algorithms.
related_patterns_notes.proxy: Proxy uses delegation to stand in for another object - typically to control access (lazy initialization, access rights, remote calls). The structural form is identical to Decorator. The distinction is intent: a proxy controls when or whether the real object is accessed; a decorator adds behaviour to a real object that is always present.
related_patterns_notes.template-method: Template Method uses inheritance and override to let a subclass fill in steps of an algorithm defined in the base class. Delegation achieves a similar effect by letting the wrapper call a delegate's operations in a fixed order, but the delegate's own self-calls do not see the wrapper's overrides. Inheritance's open-recursion (`this` dispatch) is what Template Method relies on; delegation does not provide that without explicit receiver-passing.
related_patterns_notes.servant: Servant provides behaviour to a group of classes that implement an interface (IServiced), rather than wrapping one specific class. A Servant is injected into or known by its serviced objects, which delegate requests to it on demand. Delegation wraps a specific delegate inside a wrapper; Servant provides behaviour from the outside to multiple recipients. The servant pattern is a form of delegation where the servant is the delegate and the serviced objects are the wrappers.
related_patterns_notes.chain-of-responsibility: Chain of Responsibility also uses delegation — a request is passed along a chain of handlers until one handles it. The difference is intent: delegation is about reusing behaviour by forwarding to a delegate, while Chain of Responsibility is about decoupling sender and receiver by giving multiple objects a chance to handle the request. Delegation typically has one clear delegate per wrapper; Chain of Responsibility has a dynamic chain of candidates. The structural form is similar but the purpose (decoupling vs. reuse) differs.
related_patterns_notes.facade: Facade uses delegation to provide a simplified interface over a complex subsystem, forwarding calls to the subsystem's components. The distinction is intent: Facade simplifies and narrows a complex system to make it easier to use (one-way convenience), while delegation wraps a single delegate to reuse its behaviour and often maintains the same interface. A Facade may delegate to many components; a delegation wrapper typically delegates to one. Both patterns reduce coupling but Facade is about simplification, delegation is about reuse.
related_patterns_notes.composite: Composite and delegation interact when a composite node delegates operations to its children or to a shared component. The composite pattern itself is about structuring objects into tree hierarchies where a container and its leaves share an interface; delegation is the mechanism a composite node often uses to forward operations to child nodes. Every composite uses delegation structurally (parent delegates to children), but not all delegation is compositional. The distinction is intent: Composite solves the part-whole hierarchy problem; delegation solves the code-reuse-without-inheritance problem.

anti_patterns: Delegation by inheritance: reusing a class's implementation through private/protected inheritance (plus `using` declarations to expose selected members), which re-couples the wrapper to the base's implementation and keeps the fragile-base-class problem the pattern was meant to remove.
The hand-written shim: forwarding every member of a wide interface by hand (or from a copy-pasted template) where the platform could generate it or the interface should be narrowed instead.

The middle man: a wrapper whose every member just calls the same-named delegate member, adding indirection without behaviour - the classic Lazy Class / Middle Man refactoring smell. Refactoring: expose the delegate via a getter and let clients call it directly, or collapse the wrapper if it adds nothing.
Two copies of the truth: the wrapper reimplements a member instead of forwarding it, so wrapper and delegate drift apart and callers get different behaviour depending on which type they hold.

Delegation as a substitute for a subtype relationship: the wrapper is not substitutable (callers downcast, test `instanceof`/`as?`, or the wrapper refuses members the delegate supports), which means the design wanted inheritance or a separate interface.

Accumulated forwarding debt: the delegate's interface grows with each release and hand-written forwarders are updated lazily or not at all, silently dropping newly added members until call sites fail at runtime.

Serialization proxy gotcha: Java's serialization proxy pattern (ObjectInputStream/ObjectOutputStream) can be confused with delegation but operates only during marshalling — relying on it as a delegation mechanism produces confusing code.

Trait re-use via delegation that should be a mixin: in languages with traits or mixins (Ruby, PHP, Scala), reusing a trait by delegation instead of mixing it in loses the composability and linearization semantics the trait system provides.
design_principles: Favor object composition over class inheritance (Design Patterns, p. 20) - delegation is the mechanism that makes composition as powerful for reuse as inheritance.
Program to an interface, not an implementation: wrapper and delegate share an abstraction, which is what makes the delegate replaceable and the wrapper substitutable.
Single responsibility: the delegate owns the work, the wrapper owns when, how and under which conditions the work is invoked.
Open/closed principle: new behaviour arrives as another wrapper instead of an edit to the reused class.
Information hiding: expose only the members the client needs, so the rest of the delegate's surface stays private.

Interface segregation: prefer many small interfaces that the wrapper can implement than one large interface that forces the wrapper to forward members it does not need, which is how the middle man smell starts.
best_practices: Inject the delegate (constructor, setter or DI container) instead of constructing it inside the wrapper, so the seam can be substituted in tests and at configuration time.
Prefer the generated forwarding mechanism where one exists (Kotlin `by`, Go embedding, Ruby `Forwardable`, a delegation macro), and override only the members that differ.
Keep the wrapper's exposed surface minimal - forward only the members the clients actually use; forwarding unused members creates a middle man and an interface-coupling maintenance burden.

Decide and document receiver semantics: state whether the delegate may call back into the wrapper, and pass the receiver or a callback if it must. Without an explicit receiver pass, self-calls inside the delegate stay with the delegate.
Make ownership explicit - who constructs, owns, shares and disposes the delegate - and keep a single owner for mutable delegates to avoid surprising aliasing effects.
Test the contract at the wrapper boundary, where behaviour changes, and keep generated forwarders only for interfaces that are stable.
When the delegate's interface is wide and evolving, narrow the wrapper's surface to only what clients need rather than forwarding everything - this limits the blast radius of interface changes.
For thread-safe use of mutable delegates, prefer giving each wrapper its own instance, or use immutable delegates (value objects or stateless strategy objects).

Treat the delegation interface like any other API: review it for interface segregation, document its contract, and do not expose the delegate reference unless the client genuinely needs direct access to it (see Hide Delegate refactoring).

Use Python's __getattr__ for generic delegation: when the wrapper's interface is unknown or open-ended, __getattr__ forwards attribute lookups automatically; be aware it does not override explicitly defined methods and that Fast.ai's GetAttr pattern solves the attribute-shadowing problem.

Prefer interface-based delegation over raw object composition: define a protocol/interface that both wrapper and delegate implement, making the seam explicit and type-checkable (e.g., Kotlin interface + `by`, Java interface + field injection).

Apply the 'Hide Delegate' refactoring when appropriate: if the wrapper merely exposes a delegate's interface without adding behaviour, consider returning the delegate directly to clients instead of maintaining the forwarding indirection.
Consider Kotlin `by` or Go embedding for zero-boilerplate delegation: these language mechanisms generate forwarders at compile time and eliminate the maintenance burden of hand-written forwarding.

Use delegation for extension without modification: when you cannot change a class (vendor SDK, final class, legacy code), wrap it and forward only the methods you need — this is the Adapter+Delegation pattern for third-party integration.
Document delegation intent in class-level docstrings: explicitly state which interface is being delegated, to which implementation, and why — this prevents accidental misuse as the codebase evolves.
